sentences.text: Sabinosuchus coahuilensis is a genus of mesoeucrocodylian, a type of crocodile relative, named after the town of Sabinas and the Greek word for crocodile, Souchos. The species name indicates its origin in the state of Coahuila, Mexico.

This animal possessed a longirostrine skull, meaning it had a proportionally long and slender snout. Its nasal bones were the most ornamented part of the skull, featuring unfused structures covered in teardrop-shaped pits.

The lower jaw was substantial, measuring approximately 92 cm in length, with less than half forming the central symphysis. A well-preserved section of the jaw held nineteen tooth sockets, which rose to twenty-one after a later re-examination. Most of these sockets were circular and ranged in diameter from 2.2 to 4.4 cm.
The teeth were generally robust and curved slightly toward the snout tip, but those in the rear jaw, from the seventeenth tooth onward, showed more developed curvature and compression.
The nasal bones of this crocodile relative are the most ornamented skull bone known, covered in unique teardrop-shaped pits.
Its lower jaw is exceptionally large, reaching a length of approximately 92 cm.
Amateur paleontologists from the group Palaeontologos Aficionados de Sabinas A.C. discovered the fossils in Mexico in 2002, and all specimens were later donated to the El Museo Muzquiz.

All known fossils come from the Maastrichtian Escondido Formation, though earlier reports incorrectly placed them in the Olmos Formation. The main specimen, reassembled into an almost complete form, was catalogued as PAS 945 to PAS 949 and PAS 952. A second specimen, consisting of a rostrum fragment and an articulated mandible piece, is catalogued as PAS 950 and PAS 951.
Sabinosuchus belongs to the class Reptilia and is classified within the parent group Pholidosauridae.
The genus was first described as a dyrosaurid in 2016 but was later reclassified as a pholidosaurid in 2020.
Sabinosuchus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
The original assignment of Sabinosuchus to Dyrosauridae was poorly supported according to its describers.
